text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
For a man who's had the sort of political fortnight John Howard had been blessed with you would think his end-of-year "state of the nation" style address would have been a little more inspiring.
"In looking to the future, we know that we have established a secure base camp as we climb a high mountain. We know that we must continue to go forward and that we must do so together."
A gift for Kim Beazley: "Climbing every mountain, fording every stream, follow every rainbow 'til we find our dream," he retorted.

Banalities aside, Howard's speech was a rapid-fire manifesto of self-congratulation when it wasn't making nasty references to the former Labor administration and the efforts of the current Opposition.

There was just one initiative. "...I announce today I will be appointing to my office a Major Projects Facilitator. The role of that person will be to ensure that speedy approvals are given to major investment proposals which conform with government policy."
In reply, Beazley had nothing of substance to contribute, the highlight a call for the sacking of Employment and Education Minister Amanda Vanstone and Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
Very average politics all round in the period when the breaks just kept on coming for the government.

The clouds parted dramatically in the Senate (making all those threats of a double dissolution look a bit silly), the Reserve Bank sprung another half a percentage point interest rate cut when most commentators had given up on Treasurer Peter Costello's visit from the monetary Santa.
And, again defying the forecasters, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate went down by 0.3 of a percentage point, rather than remaining stuck on 8.8 percent.
It was an end-of-year to dream of.
But there was little spark on either side of the Parliament, exhaustion setting in at the end of the year which bought a change of leaders on both sides and a change of government.

Obviously Labor had more reason for introspection. The party has yet to begin the policy formulation task which it must complete next year before the January, 1998 national conference in Hobart. This will be the biggest policy upheaval for many years as the blueprint which evolved during the 13 years in government is restructured for Opposition.
If the medium-term outlook is not daunting enough, consider the short-term prospect for Labor.
On Saturday, the West Australian state election is certain to deliver another electoral blow for Labor but particularly for the federal leader.
A West Australian himself, the party's own polling suggests the result in the seat coinciding with Beazley's own will run strongly against Labor.
At least one federal Labor front bencher was absent from Parliament House in Canberra this week as the party put all hands to the wheel in Perth.
The leadership will argue that state elections have no federal implications.
They know, however, that a landslide in the West will put yet another hold in Labor's morale, and dent the Beazley armour.
That will come on top of a series of polls which have Howard's coalition strengthening despite the pain of the first Costello budget. It's Labor that has mountains to climb.
The Coalition, meanwhile, is on a roll.
Howard will preside over the final Cabinet meeting of the year next Monday and Tuesday.
In line with the experience of this government over the past nine months there will be as much politics on the agenda as policy.
This is a very political government. Every decision is put through the political spectrometer and policies already made are marketed to make the most political impact.
On Monday, Howard and Costello will relaunch the so-called family tax initiative which will deliver tax cuts to single income families earning under A$68,000 a year.
The package has already been twice around the arena -- first, with much fanfare, during the election campaign, with a repeat in the August budget.
It's not all plain sailing for Howard. Beazley's right about Senator Vanstone, at least.
She's a danger to herself and the Ministers around her. Downer has his head down determined to cling to his ministry.
While there is a case for a reshuffle, the word from inside the Howard office is there won't be one.
The Prime Minister is no Malcolm Fraser. Ministers won't be moved on without significant cause. And Opposition calls for changes will only entrench Howard's Ministry.
As Parliament grinds to an end, it's also grinding Labor into the political dust.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
